Mexican lotería is played with picture cards: El Gallo, La Muerte, El Valiente. This deck holds the fears people have about dying and growing old. One card a day. Turn it over and look the fear in the eye.
Tap the card to turn it over
Tried. That\'s how a fear gets smaller.

A calaverita literaria is a short, funny poem in which La Catrina comes to fetch someone. In Mexico they are written about friends, teachers and presidents every November. Write one about yourself: laughing at the end takes away some of its power.
No verses yet. Start from one of Catrina\'s examples if the first line won\'t come.
La Flaca came for me one day…
Rhyme if you can, but funny beats perfect. Who comes for you, what are you busy with, and how do you talk your way out?
The paper is folded. Draw with your finger to cut it.
It\'s hanging. It will flutter for a week, then the wind takes it, like everything.

Papel picado hangs over every fiesta and every altar. It is meant to tear and fade: beautiful because it doesn\'t last.

The psychiatrist Irvin Yalom called it rippling: we go on in the people we have touched, often without knowing. Cempasúchil petals light the souls\' way home. Each marigold here is someone or something that carries a trace of you.
taught her to ride a bike
No marigolds yet. Think small: a recipe you passed on, a tree you planted, a friend you talked out of a bad idea.
Eight statements. Say how true each is for you right now. Once a month is enough: the point is to watch the line go down.
Cool. Death is a fact you can look at without flinching. Keep visiting.
Warm. The fear is there but it doesn\'t run the house. The lotería cards work best now.
Hot. The fear is loud. Go gently: a card a day, a candle, a verse. And talk to someone if it weighs on your days.

resources.string: Ageing isn\'t a slow goodbye. For many people it was when the real work began.

In a study that followed people for over twenty years, the Yale researcher Becca Levy found that those who thought well of getting older lived on average 7.5 years longer than those who dreaded it. How you see ageing is part of how you age.

string-array.item: Took up painting seriously in her late seventies, when her hands grew too stiff for embroidery. She painted for another twenty years and became one of America\'s best-loved artists.
Finished Falstaff, his only great comedy and one of his finest operas, at seventy-nine. His funniest work came last.
Published the first of the Little House books at sixty-five, after a life as a farmer\'s wife. The series is still read by children everywhere.
Published his Thesaurus at seventy-three, after a career in medicine. He kept revising it until he died at ninety.
Became president of South Africa at seventy-five, after twenty-seven years in prison.
Took up running in his eighties after losing his wife and son, and ran his first marathon at eighty-nine.
Made The Great Wave around seventy, and wrote at seventy-five that nothing he had drawn before seventy was worth noticing.
A schoolteacher for thirty years, he published his first book, Angela\'s Ashes, at sixty-six. It won the Pulitzer Prize.

resources.string: In Mexico, death isn\'t hidden away. On the Day of the Dead people build altars, dress up as skeletons, eat sugar skulls and write funny poems about their own funerals. Calavera brings that spirit to your phone, to make the end a little less frightening and life a little brighter.
This is you, without the skin. It sways, dances when tapped, and grows older with you: every birthday Catrina brings a new privilege of years.
For your age and birthday presents. Optional.
A hat and a painted face to start. The rest of the wardrobe is paid for in marigold petals, earned by the practices.
Calavera is for making peace with mortality someday. If thoughts of ending your life are about now, please talk to someone today. There\'s a link to helplines in the settings.
One quiet notice a day with her word. Nothing else.
Everything is kept on this phone only. A backup is one zip with the ofrenda, its photos, your verses and your wardrobe.

string-array.name: fear_reflections
string-array.item: Ay, mi vida, everyone gets forgotten eventually, even pharaohs. But look closer: you remember your great-grandmother\'s soup without remembering her name. Who we are travels in what we did, not in the name on the stone. You\'re being remembered right now, in a hundred small ways you can\'t see.

You worry about the nothing after. Tell me, did the billions of years before you were born trouble you? Epicurus said it well: where death is, I am not; where I am, death is not. Nothingness can\'t hurt anyone, because there\'s no one there to hurt. What frightens you is losing this, so love it while you have it.

Pain is a fair worry, and an honest one. But medicine for the end has grown wise: palliative care exists so that the last days can be calm. Fear of pain is often worse than pain itself, because it lasts all your life instead of a few days. Know your options, write down your wishes, and put the fear down.

Nobody gets enough time, querido. Kings and beggars all left with things undone. The trick isn\'t more time; it\'s noticing the time you have. Four thousand weeks, give or take. How many of them did you actually look at?

You fear needing help one day. But you needed help to be born, to eat, to walk, and nobody thought less of you. Being cared for is part of life\'s circle, not a failure at its end. Practise receiving now: let someone help you this week and say only gracias.

Wrinkles, grey hair, a softer jaw. That face is a map of every laugh and every squint into the sun. Nobody looks at an old oak and thinks it failed to stay a sapling. And look at me: no face at all, and I\'m the most elegant woman at every party.

This is the fear that comes from love, and so it\'s the most honourable. You will lose people, and they will lose you. That\'s why the ofrenda exists: love doesn\'t stop at the grave, it just changes address. Say the things now, so later there are only good memories to set on the altar.

Everyone leaves something half done: a book, a garden, a quarrel. That\'s not failure, that\'s proof you were still living. Pick one thing that really matters and finish it. Forgive yourself the rest.

Dying alone frightens many. But consider: most fear isn\'t about the last hour, it\'s about feeling unloved. You can tend to that today. Call someone. Write a letter. The ones who die surrounded are the ones who spent years gathering people, one small kindness at a time.

Did I live right? Everyone asks at the end. Nurses who sit with the dying hear the same regrets: I wish I\'d lived true to myself, worked less, kept in touch with friends, let myself be happier. The good news is that you\'re not at the end. You can still change the answers.

What\'s behind the door? Nobody really knows, not the priests, not the scientists, not even me, and I\'m the one holding it open. Some find peace in faith, some in the thought of returning to the stars. The unknown is also where every good surprise of your life came from.

The body is a borrowed house, and one day the landlord comes back. It creaks, it leaks, the stairs get steep. But it carried you to every dance and every embrace. Thank it instead of blaming it. Bones like mine are what\'s left, and look how well they dance.

string-array.name: fear_exercises
string-array.item: Write down three things you learned from someone who is gone. Notice: they live on in you.
Lie down for two minutes and think of the night sky before you were born. Calm, wasn\'t it? Then open your eyes and look at something beautiful.
Find out, in two minutes of reading, what palliative care offers where you live. Knowing beats imagining.
Count how many weeks you\'ve lived (years × 52). Then choose one thing to do this week that you\'ll be glad of.
Let someone help you today, with anything at all, and answer only: gracias.
Look in the mirror for one minute and find three things time gave you, not took.
Send one message today to someone you love, saying exactly why.
Write down the one unfinished thing that matters most. Then write the next tiny step and do it today.
Call someone you haven\'t spoken to in a while. Just to hear how they are.
Finish this sentence three times: if I had a year left, I would…
Recall a time when something unknown turned out wonderfully. Write it down in one line.
Before sleep, thank your body for one thing it did today. Out loud, if you dare.

string-array.name: catrina_words
string-array.item: Death is not the opposite of life. It\'s the frame that makes the picture.
Everyone you\'ve ever admired was going to die too. It didn\'t stop them.
Memento mori isn\'t a threat, cariño. It\'s a reminder to eat dessert.
An old tree isn\'t a failed young one.
The dead want two things from you: to be remembered, and for you to enjoy yourself.
Every day you\'re the oldest you\'ve ever been and the youngest you\'ll ever be.
Fear of death is mostly fear of not having lived. Fix that part.
I come for everyone. That\'s the most democratic thing in the world.
The Stoics said: practise letting go of small things, and the big one will be easier.
A wrinkle is where a smile has been.
Nobody on their last day wished they\'d answered more emails.
The petals fall, the flower doesn\'t mind. It was busy being a flower.
You will die, yes. But not today, so what are you doing with today?
Ageing is a privilege denied to many. Wear it like a good hat.
Grief is love with nowhere to go. Give it somewhere: a candle, a story, a recipe.
The skeleton is the only outfit that suits everyone.
Worrying about the end steals the middle.
Plant a tree whose shade you will never sit in. That\'s how the old outwit me.
Laugh at me. I don\'t mind. Laughter is how people get brave.
In Mexico they say you die three times: when the heart stops, when you\'re buried, and when nobody remembers you. Work on the third.
Slow down. You\'re not late for anything except your own life.
Your bones have danced with you since before you could walk. Be nice to them.
The best way to prepare for death is to love life well. Lucky you: that\'s also the best way to live.
Nothing lasts, and that\'s exactly why it\'s precious.
You are made of atoms forged in stars. Death just returns the loan.
Elders aren\'t people who ran out of future. They\'re people who collected more past.
Say the kind thing now. The funeral is too late for it.
The candle doesn\'t mourn that it burns. It just gives light.
You can\'t add days to your life, but you can add life to your days.
Hasta la muerte, todo es vida. Until death, everything is life.

string-array.name: catrina_errands
string-array.item: Take one photo today of something you\'ll miss when you\'re old.
Eat something slowly, paying full attention, as if it were your last time.
Tell someone older than you one thing you admire about them.
Look at the sky for one full minute.
Ask an old person a question about their youth, and listen to the whole answer.
Do one thing today that your eighty-year-old self would thank you for.
Put on music you loved at sixteen and dance to one song.
Throw away or give away one thing you\'ve been keeping "just in case".
Write a thank-you note to someone. You don\'t have to send it.
Walk somewhere without your phone for fifteen minutes.
Notice three things today that are beautiful because they won\'t last.
Cook or bake something from a family recipe.
Call a grandparent, a parent or an old friend. Just to talk.
Say "I don\'t know" out loud at least once today, and enjoy it.
Forgive one small thing: someone else\'s, or your own.
Put a flower or a candle somewhere you\'ll see it this evening.
Go to bed fifteen minutes earlier. Bones need their rest.
Tell a story about someone who is gone, to someone who never met them.
Look in the mirror and smile at the person getting older there.
Laugh at something on purpose: a film, a joke, yourself.
Spend ten minutes doing nothing at all. Practise being still.
Stretch for five minutes and thank each joint by name.
Hug someone a few seconds longer than usual.
Write down one thing you want to learn when you\'re old.
Step outside tonight and find the brightest star.
Ask someone how they want to be remembered. Then answer it yourself.
Send a message to someone you\'ve lost touch with.
Light a candle and sit with it for two minutes.
Do one brave little thing you\'ve been putting off.
Finish the day by naming three good things it held.

string-array.name: cal_examples
string-array.item:
La Flaca came for {name}, late,
and found them busy with a plate.
"Sit down," said {name}, "have a bite!"
Now Death drops round on Friday night.

Here lies {name}, who was sure
they'd find the time to clean the floor.
They never did. The dust remains.
They danced instead. No one complains.

Death knocked on {name}'s door at three.
"Not now," said {name}, "I'm making tea."
She waited. Tea turned into lunch.
Now Death and {name} have Sunday brunch.

When Catrina called for {name} at last,
she asked, "Your life, did it go fast?"
"Too fast," said {name}, "but what a ride!
One more dance, and then we'll glide."
